questions.explanation: ping sends ICMP Echo Requests and times the Echo Replies. ICMP is its own layer-3 protocol, not TCP or UDP.

questions.prompt: You can ping 1.1.1.1 successfully but 'ping example.com' fails with 'name or service not known'. What is broken?
questions.explanation: Reaching a raw IP proves connectivity works; failing on a name means DNS resolution is the problem.

questions.prompt: The router a host uses to reach destinations outside its local network is called the default ____.
questions.explanation: The default gateway is the exit point to other networks; you find it in 'ip route' as 'default via ...'.

questions.prompt: Which statements about ping and ICMP are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: 'time=' in ping output is the round-trip time (RTT)
Many hosts and firewalls deliberately drop ICMP
No ping reply always proves the host is powered off
Pinging a raw IP tests connectivity without involving DNS

questions.explanation: RTT is the 'time=' value, ICMP is often blocked, and pinging an IP avoids DNS. A blocked ping does not prove the host is down.

questions.prompt: Order the bottom-up troubleshooting steps from nearest to farthest.

items.text: Interface up and has an IP
Reach the internet by raw IP

questions.explanation: Test from closest to farthest — interface, gateway, internet-by-IP, DNS, then the service; the first failure localizes the problem.

questions.prompt: Match each command to what it shows.

pairs.right: The routing table and default gateway

questions.explanation: ip addr shows addresses, ip route shows routes/gateway, ping tests reachability, and curl tests the real application service.
